sum: Canadian Natural Resources (TSX:CNQ) just put fresh Q3 2026 numbers on the table, with revenue of CA$12.8b and net income of CA$3.0b, giving investors plenty to reassess.

Canadian Natural Resources shares have pulled back over the past week, with a 7 day share price return of down 12.65%, even as fresh Q3 headlines highlighted stronger production, higher net income and a commitment to channel all free cash flow into buybacks and dividends. That short term wobble sits against a 45.37% year to date share price return and a 60.83% 1 year total shareholder return. This points to momentum that has been strong overall but is now being tested as investors weigh how sustainable these earnings and capital returns might be.

Canadian Natural Resources looks like a powerhouse on recent earnings and cash returns, yet the 12.65% pullback asks a simple question: Are you looking at strength on sale or a full price tag?

On Simply Wall St's most followed view, Canadian Natural Resources screens as undervalued, with a fair value of about CA$75.10 compared to the last close at CA$68.50. That gap sits on top of a record of strong earnings, generous capital returns and a formal free cash flow framework that Q3 2026 has just put back in the spotlight.

The updated free cash flow allocation policy, which now directs 75% of free cash flow to shareholders once net debt falls below $16b and 100% once it reaches $13b, sets up a framework in which future cash generation is increasingly tied to dividends and buybacks, with potential implications for earnings per share and equity valuation.

Canadian Natural Resources stock signals stronger 2027 buyback outlook
sum: Canadian Natural Resources shifted investor attention from its third-quarter earnings to the durability of its capital-return plan after management said on Thursday, November 5, that buybacks could continue at a similar pace into 2027 if free cash flow remains strong. The comment adds a forward-looking detail to the company's plan to direct 100% of free cash flow to repurchases, subject to market conditions.

On the earnings call, President Scott Stauth said the planned monthly repurchase pace should not be viewed as a two-month trial. He expects the company to continue at a similar rate into the new year while commodity prices and free cash flow remain supportive. The full transcript is available from Yahoo Finance.

Canadian Natural reached its CAD 13 billion net debt target earlier than expected, ending the quarter at CAD 12.1 billion. The company targets CAD 800 million of share repurchases in each of November and December, while management said the pace could change if commodity prices shift materially.

The Horizon oil sands turnaround was completed in 28 days, seven days ahead of schedule. Management expects the earlier completion to add 23,000 barrels per day of high-margin synthetic crude production in the fourth quarter and has extended the planned interval between turnarounds from two years to three years.

Canadian Natural also reported record quarterly thermal in situ production of approximately 300,000 barrels per day and record North American conventional liquids production of approximately 358,000 barrels per day. Management expects a strong fourth quarter, supported by oil sands mining and upgrading, thermal operations and execution across its portfolio.

Canadian Natural Resources stock faces Q3 earnings test on November 5
sum: Canadian Natural Resources is approaching its third-quarter report with expectations for stronger year-over-year earnings, but the preview from Zacks Equity Research, published by Yahoo Finance on November 3, does not point to a clear earnings beat. The company is scheduled to release results before the market opens on Thursday, November 5.

Zacks puts its third-quarter estimate at 1.05 dollars per share and revenue of 8.3 billion dollars. The earnings estimate is 69.4 percent above the year-earlier level, while the revenue forecast implies 20 percent growth. At the same time, the earnings consensus has been reduced by 7.9 percent over the past 30 days, raising the importance of the final operating figures.

Canadian Natural Resources enters the release after adjusted earnings per share of 1.58 dollars in the second quarter, above the 1.43-dollar consensus estimate cited by Zacks. Second-quarter revenue was reported at 10.6 billion dollars against a 9.2-billion-dollar estimate. Zacks said the company had exceeded consensus earnings estimates in each of the previous four quarters, with an average surprise of 12.9 percent.

The preview identifies several potential supports for the quarter. Canadian Natural Resources has raised its 2026 production guidance, while output from Jackfish and volumes from acquired assets could bolster earnings. Operating efficiencies and possible cost savings of 10 percent or more at Peace River may also support profitability.

Commodity pricing remains a counterweight. Management expects synthetic crude pricing to moderate from the second quarter premium of 8.37 dollars per barrel over West Texas Intermediate toward parity or a modest premium. That shift could reduce realized prices and profitability. Planned maintenance extending through the third quarter and into early fourth quarter may also constrain production and lift expenses.

Zacks also points to the company's capital expenditure program of approximately 6 billion Canadian dollars for 2026. Weaker commodity prices would increase pressure on free cash flow, although the preview says operating improvements could provide support. Its model does not conclusively predict an earnings beat for this release.

Toronto Stock Exchange Today: S&P/TSX Composite Rises 0.51% to 35,801.09 as Trade Deal Hopes Offset Energy Slump
sum: Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index closed 0.51% higher at 35,801.09 on Monday 2 November 2026, recovering part of Friday's steep loss as financials, materials and industrials led gains and President Trump said a framework for a new trade deal with Canada was in place, while energy producers slumped with oil.

The S&P/TSX Composite Index, the main benchmark of the Toronto Stock Exchange, closed at 35,801.09 on Monday, up 181.06 points or 0.51% from Friday's close of 35,620.03. The blue-chip S&P/TSX 60 rose 0.49% to 2,135.53.

The index gave back roughly half of its earlier gains. It was up more than 330 points at around 35,950 in early afternoon, before easing as US technology stocks turned lower. Even so, Toronto outperformed the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, both of which finished in negative territory, helped by its smaller exposure to large technology companies.

Financials, materials, industrials and real estate led the advance, with Royal Bank of Canada up 0.8% and Bank of Montreal up 1.1%. Gold recovered from recent lows, with December futures up 1.35% to $3,951.50 an ounce, supporting miners after last week's heavy selling. Trade news provided an additional boost: President Donald Trump said his administration had set up a framework for a new trade agreement with Canada, and Prime Minister Mark Carney described the discussions as constructive. Formal negotiations are expected to resume this week.

Domestic data also helped. Ottawa's federal deficit narrowed to C$223 million in August as revenues rose 7.1%, easing concerns about government borrowing. The S&P/TSX 60 VIX volatility gauge fell 2% to 15.71, signalling calmer conditions after Friday's steepest one-day decline in nearly six months.

The top gainers were spread across sectors. Colliers International rose 7.90% to C$145.98, Aecon Group climbed 7.84% to C$53.09 and Curaleaf Holdings gained 8.50% to C$12.77. Industrial and construction names benefited from improving trade sentiment and lower fuel costs.

Energy producers were the biggest losers as oil collapsed. Baytex Energy fell 9.77% to C$6.79, Strathcona Resources dropped 9.45% to C$38.82 and Vermilion Energy slid 8.52% to C$17.50. Index heavyweight Canadian Natural Resources fell 4.2%.

3 TSX Dividend Stocks for Reliable Passive Income
sum: If you’re looking for reliable passive income, consider high-quality TSX dividend stocks. Notably, Canadian companies with a proven record of maintaining or increasing their dividends through different market cycles are dependable investments. These TSX stocks are backed by strong fundamentals, established operations, consistent earnings growth, and a sustainable payout ratio.
With this background, here are three TSX dividend stocks for reliable passive income.

TC Energy (TSX: TRP) is a reliable dividend stock worth holding for passive income. Its relatively stable operations, predictable cash flow, and long-standing dividend growth history support its investment case.

TC Energy operates natural gas transportation and storage infrastructure while also investing in power generation. A large portion of its earnings comes from regulated businesses and long-term contracts, including take-or-pay agreements with financially strong customers. About 98% of its comparable EBITDA comes from regulated assets or contractual arrangements, helping reduce exposure to commodity-price swings and economic volatility. This enables it to keep paying and increasing dividends.

TC Energy has increased its annual dividend for 26 consecutive years. Further, management expects its dividends to rise by approximately 3% to 5% annually in the years ahead, providing investors with steadily growing passive income.

Looking ahead, TC Energy’s long-life infrastructure assets, supported by long-term commercial arrangements, are likely to drive its financials and dividend payments. TC Energy also has a solid investment pipeline. Its $22 billion secured capital program through 2031 will support its earnings growth and dividend payouts.

TC Energy’s relatively predictable cash flow, a long record of dividend increases, exposure to growing natural gas demand, and a substantial pipeline of secured projects make it a reliable income stock.

Best Canadian Oil Stocks to Buy in 2026
sum: - Energy still prints cash: Even with oil prices bouncing around, Canadian producers have gotten disciplined about capital allocation, returning serious money to shareholders through buybacks and dividends rather than chasing growth at any cost.

- Size and strategy vary widely: This list spans everything from Canadian Natural Resources, a blue-chip giant with decades of reserves, to smaller names like Valeura Energy and Tenaz Energy that are building value through international acquisitions and unconventional strategies most investors overlook.

- Commodity prices dictate everything: No matter how well-run these companies are, a sustained drop in oil prices compresses margins fast. Keep an eye on global demand signals, OPEC+ decisions, and each company’s breakeven costs before sizing your position too aggressively.

Energy is the one sector where I tell people to stop watching the price of the stock and start watching the price of the barrel. WTI dictates almost everything here, and right now investors are stuck trying to figure out if oil is range-bound for good or just catching its breath before the next leg. That uncertainty is exactly why I think you need to be picky about which names you own in this space.

The six companies on this list aren’t interchangeable, even though they all get lumped into the same “oil stocks” bucket. Suncor Energy and Imperial Oil run integrated models, pulling oil out of the ground and refining it into something you can actually put in your car, which smooths out some of the pain when crude prices dip. Canadian Natural Resources is the production machine of the group, and I’ve written before about whether it’s still Canada’s darling producer after years of aggressive growth.

Cenovus Energy sits somewhere in between, with a refining arm that’s grown into a real asset after some messy years, and I’ve dug into whether it’s the best oil and gas play on the TSX right now. Then you’ve got the smaller names. Valeura Energy is building a production base in Turkey, about as far from the oil sands as you can get while still being a TSX-listed producer. Saturn Oil & Gas has grown through acquisition, picking up producing assets on the cheap and trying to turn them into free cash flow.

sum: Payouts from dividend stocks can provide a reliable source of passive income. However, because dividends are never guaranteed, it’s important to find companies with the financial strength to sustain and consistently increase their payouts over the long term.

The TSX has several high-quality dividend stocks capable of growing their dividends across various market cycles. These Canadian companies stand out as some of the best dividend stocks to own in 2026 and beyond.
With that in mind, here are five of the 0best Canadian dividend stocks that offer dependable income in 2026 and beyond.

Fortis (TSX: FTS) is one of the best Canadian dividend stocks for 2026. Its rate-regulated electricity transmission and distribution business generates predictable and growing cash flow, enabling consistent dividend growth. The utility company has increased its dividend for 52 consecutive years and is expected to extend that streak with another hike in 2026.

Fortis’s $28.8 billion capital plan will expand its regulated rate base and support low-risk earnings growth. Management projects the rate base will grow about 7% annually through 2030, supporting dividend increases of 4% to 6% per year through the end of this decade. Fortis’s defensive business model, expanding rate base, rising electricity demand, and a strong balance sheet position it well for continued dividend growth.

Enbridge (TSX: ENB) is one of the best dividend stocks to hold in 2026. It has consistently paid dividends for more than 70 years and increased it annually since 1995. The energy infrastructure giant is well-positioned to extend that streak in 2026 while offering an attractive yield of about 5%.

Its dividend is backed by a diversified revenue base, with nearly all EBITDA generated from regulated assets or long-term take-or-pay contracts. These stable cash flows reduce exposure to commodity price swings and support consistent growth in distributable cash flow. Looking ahead, strength in its core businesses, strong project backlog, and rising energy demand position Enbridge well to deliver future dividend growth.

items.t: 3 Canadian Dividend Stocks to Own for Decades
sum: Canadian investors are searching for good TSX dividend stocks to add to their self-directed Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA) or Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP) portfolio focused on generating income and long-term total returns.
With markets near record levels and trade uncertainty threatening the economy, it makes sense to consider companies that can deliver steady dividend growth through the full economic cycle.
Fortis (TSX: FTS) is a good example of a top TSX dividend-growth stock that investors can buy and sit on for years.

The company owns utility businesses across Canada and in the United States, with nearly all of the revenue coming from rate-regulated assets. These operations include power generation facilities, natural gas distribution utilities, and electricity transmission grids that provide essential power services.

Fortis continues to expand its portfolio with a current $28.8 billion capital program that is expected to boost the rate base from $42 billion to nearly $58 billion over five years. As the new assets are completed and begin to earn revenue, the increase in cash flow should enable Fortis to meet its target of 4% to 6% annual dividend increases through 2030. Fortis raised the distribution in each of the past 52 years.
Enbridge (TSX: ENB) has increased its dividend for 31 consecutive years. The stock is up about 26% in the past 12 months, but still offers new investors a dividend yield of close to 5% today.

Enbridge is benefiting from its strategy pivot over the past few years that saw the company allocate growth investments to emerging opportunities in the North American energy sector, particularly in the United States. Management spent US$3 billion to buy an oil export facility in Texas and another US$14 billion to acquire three American natural gas utilities. Enbridge is also a partner on the Woodfibre liquefied natural gas (LNG) export facility nearing completion on the coast of British Columbia.

items.t: 3 Canadian Dividend Stocks Quietly Raising Payouts
sum: Dividend stocks can be powerful long-term wealth creators, as investors could benefit from both capital appreciation and a steady stream of dividend income. While dividends are never guaranteed, companies with established business models, reliable cash flows, and strong financial positions are better equipped to sustain and grow their payouts over time. Regular dividend increases also reflect the strength of a company's underlying business and management's confidence in its future cash flow generation.
With that in mind, here are three Canadian companies that have consistently increased their dividends for many years, making them attractive options for long-term investors.

Fortis (TSX:FTS), one of Canada's most dependable dividend-growth stocks, is my first pick. The regulated electric and natural gas utility serves 3.5 million customers across Canada, the United States, and the Caribbean, with approximately 95% of its assets dedicated to low-risk transmission and distribution operations. This regulated business model generates stable and predictable cash flows regardless of economic conditions or commodity price fluctuations. Supported by these reliable earnings, Fortis has maintained its dividend growth for 52 consecutive years and currently offers a forward yield of 3.1%.

The utility also has a clear path to future growth. Its $28.8 billion capital investment plan could expand its rate base at a 7% annualized rate through the end of the decade, supporting steady earnings growth. At the same time, Fortis continues to improve operating efficiency through preventive maintenance programs and other cost-saving initiatives. Backed by its resilient business model, disciplined growth strategy, and strong financial foundation, Fortis's management expects to grow its dividend at an annualized rate of 4–6% through 2030, making it an excellent choice for long-term income investors.

Canadian Natural Resources (TSX:CNQ) is another high-quality dividend stock that is well-suited for income-seeking investors. The oil and natural gas company operates a portfolio of large, long-life, low-decline assets that require relatively modest capital reinvestment.

items.t: 5 Canadian Stocks Beginners Can Buy and Hold Forever
sum: One of the biggest mistakes beginners make is chasing the next hot stock. While that approach can be tempting, long-term wealth is usually built by owning top Canadian stocks and giving them time to grow.

The best Canadian stocks for beginners are the companies with proven business models, durable competitive advantages, consistent earnings growth, and the financial strength to weather economic downturns. Over time, these businesses can reward shareholders through capital appreciation, growing dividends, and compounding.
In this context, here are high-quality Canadian stocks beginners can buy and hold forever.
Fortis (TSX:FTS) could be a great choice for beginners. The utility giant offers a solid combination of income and stability, and also has significant growth prospects.

It is engaged in regulated electricity and natural gas transmission and distribution, which provides predictable revenue and robust cash flows. Since most of its earnings come from regulated operations, Fortis is less vulnerable to economic downturns, giving it stability. Thanks to its predictable cash flows, the company has increased its dividend annually for more than five decades.

Fortis will invest $28.8 billion over the next five years to expand its regulated assets, supporting future earnings and dividend growth. Growing electricity demand, asset optimization, and a strong balance sheet further strengthen its growth story.

Hydro One (TSX:H) is one of Canada's leading electricity transmission and distribution companies, and a compelling stock for beginners. Its regulated business provides stability and predictable cash flow, enabling it to reward shareholders with consistent dividend growth. Moreover, its steady earnings growth supports its share price.

items.t: 1 Canadian Dividend Stock Down 16% to Buy and Hold Forever
sum: Canadian Natural Resources (TSX:CNQ) stock has slipped 16% in June as the U.S. and Iran hold a ceasefire and allow oil ships to pass. It was known from March, when the war first began, that the negotiations would drive the price of energy stocks. The Iran war was of particular relevance to U.S. energy companies as most of their oil supply goes through the Strait of Hormuz. Hence, when the passage opened, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) prices fell 30% from $96 to below $67/barrel in June alone. Most Canadian energy companies have kept the WTI benchmark at $50/barrel.
While you know the reason for the June dip, the question is whether this dip is a buying opportunity.

As one of the world's largest oil sands reserves, Canadian Natural Resources not only has ample oil and gas to mine, but it also has the infrastructure to mine it efficiently at a cost of mid-US$40/barrel.

Canadian Natural Resources faced pressure in January when Venezuela's oil crisis opened the roads for Venezuelan oil to flow into American refineries and the global oil market. Even though Venezuela has the world's largest oil reserves, the lack of energy infrastructure makes it less accessible.

Canadian Natural Resources sustained the 2016 oil crisis when the U.S. shale gas boom reduced oil prices to US$65/barrel and lower. It has built a financial model where the mid-$40 breakeven price includes the dividend amount, allowing it to comfortably sustain dividends even when the oil price falls to US$50 WTI. Its dividend policy states that 100% of free cash flow will be allocated towards shareholder returns if net debt is $13 billion or lower. It has been buying new reserves in 2024 and 2025 and using the incremental sales to repay debt. At the end of the first quarter of 2026, it had debt of $17.4 billion and is looking to pay down debt further.

Canadian Natural Resources benefited from higher volumes in the first quarter, driving its adjusted funds from operations up 17% sequentially. It will benefit from a higher oil price in the second quarter, which could keep cash flow high. Such supply shocks helped it absorb the entry of Venezuelan oil into global markets.
